paragraphs: Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashia of Dewil.

He was a student of Rav, as is explicit in Niddah 26b: Shmuel and the students of Rav and Rav Yehuda were sitting, and Rav Yosef son of Rav Menashia of Dewil passed by them. Shmuel said to him: What did Rav say about the afterbirth? And in Kiddushin 79b he acted in accordance with Rav, and Shmuel was angered at him and said: Everyone measures for him with the small measure, but this one of the rabbis measures for him with the large measure. And in Gittin 81a he sent to Shmuel, 'Let our master teach us.' Hyman maintains that this was, without doubt, after Rav’s death, and in Sura no head of the academy had been appointed, and there was only a group of sages there, and all their doubts they sent to Shmuel. And in Ketubot 65a it is told that his wife came after his death before Rav Yosef; she said to him: Assign me sustenance — assign me silk garments, etc. Hyman suggests that he had married her in his old age and that she was young, explaining her request for silk garments.[^1][^2][^3]

notes.text: The Rav Yosef who receives the widow’s requests is distinct from her deceased husband. “Sustenance” and “silk garments” are her requests, not the judge’s.
The small/large measure phrase is Shmuel’s reported idiom about the degree of deference shown to Rav; it is preserved without turning it into an actual payment or measured commodity.

בל״ס means “without doubt”: this is Hyman’s stated certainty about the post-Rav date and Sura’s leadership. His explanation that the widow was young and had married an elderly husband is separately tentative. References and the Dewil place form follow Hyman.
